parts.title: Booking a balloon flight
parts.context: A man books a hot-air balloon flight as a birthday present.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a company to book a hot-air balloon flight. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: Skyhigh Balloon Flights, Lucy speaking.

script.speaker: mark
script.text: Hello. I'd like to book a balloon flight, please. It's a present for my wife's birthday, and I want it to be a surprise.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: How lovely. I'll take some details first.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The flight is a birthday present, so 'birthday' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: mark
script.text: Mark Holloway. That's H-O-L-L-O-W-A-Y.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: Thank you, Mr Holloway. How many passengers will there be?

script.speaker: mark
script.text: Two, my wife and me. We did think of bringing our son, but he's too young.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: And which date would you like?

script.speaker: mark
script.text: Saturday the sixth of September, if there's space.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: There is. Flights usually start at five in the morning, but later in September the sun rises later, so we'll meet at six o'clock.

script.speaker: mark
script.text: That's early, but fine. Where do we meet?

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: At Oakfield Farm, near Bridgewater. There's a sign at the end of the lane, and our team will be there with the balloon.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: The flight itself lasts about an hour, although the whole morning takes around four hours with the preparation and the trip back.

script.speaker: mark
script.text: And the price?

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: It's ninety-five pounds each. It was ninety last year, but fuel has become more expensive.

script.speaker: mark
script.text: What should we wear?

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: Warm clothes, because it's colder in the air, and sturdy shoes, as the field can be muddy. Please don't wear sandals or high heels.

script.speaker: mark
script.text: What happens if the weather is bad?

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: Balloons can't fly in strong winds, so then we postpone the flight to another date, free of charge. We'll call you the evening before to let you know.

script.speaker: mark
script.text: Is there anything afterwards?

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: Yes. After landing, everyone gets a glass of champagne, which is a tradition among balloonists, and then a cooked breakfast at the farm.

script.speaker: mark
script.text: Wonderful. I'll make the booking now.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: Lovely. I'll just take your card details.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A visit to an aquarium
parts.context: A guide welcomes visitors to an aquarium.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a guide welcoming visitors to an aquarium. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Seaview Aquarium. I'm Priya, one of the guides. Please look at the plan in your guide. We're at the entrance, at the bottom, and the big ocean tank is straight ahead of us. Just inside the entrance, on the left, is the gift shop, which I'd save until the end.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: Let's start on the left side of the building. The room nearest the entrance is the touch pool, where you can gently touch starfish and sea urchins. Above it is the jellyfish gallery, and at the top on the left, the seahorse room.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: On the right side, the room nearest the entrance is the café, which has a lovely view of the main tank. Above it is the penguin beach, which is always popular. And at the top on the right is the shark tunnel, where you walk right under the sharks.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: Some facts. We have about four hundred species of fish here, which is more than most people expect, although most of them are quite small.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: The penguins are fed at two o'clock every day, and it's worth arriving a little early. The shark feeding is later, at four.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: At the touch pool, please wash your hands before and after you touch the animals. You don't need gloves, because they can damage the skin of the creatures.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: The jellyfish gallery is kept very dark. That's deliberate, because the special lighting makes the jellyfish stand out, and they seem to glow in the water.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: And our new project is a breeding programme for seahorses, which are quite endangered in the wild. If it works, we hope to return young seahorses to the sea. Please enjoy your visit.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A study of air quality
parts.context: Two students plan a study of air pollution in a city.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two environmental science students, Tara and Ben, planning a study of air quality in a city. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: tara
script.text: Ben, I've picked up the air quality sensors from the department. There are six, and they're smaller than I expected.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: How long do the batteries last?

script.speaker: tara
script.text: About ten days, so we'll need to recharge them in the middle of the study, which will run for a month.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Where shall we put them? I thought of the campus, because it's convenient.

script.speaker: tara
script.text: But a campus isn't typical. Dr Singh said we should choose places with different traffic levels, so I'd suggest the main road, a side street, the park and the railway station.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: We need permission to attach sensors to the lamp posts.

script.speaker: tara
script.text: The council has already agreed, but only for the main road and the park.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: What time of day should we measure?

script.speaker: tara
script.text: The sensors take a reading every minute, all day, but we'll focus on the morning rush hour, because that's when we expect pollution to peak.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: And the weather. Rain washes pollution out of the air.

script.speaker: tara
script.text: So we'll record the rainfall as well, and compare dry days with wet days.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: tara
script.text: For the background section I've made notes on the main pollutants and where they come from. Nitrogen dioxide first.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: That's mostly from traffic exhaust, especially diesel vehicles.

script.speaker: tara
script.text: Ozone?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: That's interesting, because it isn't released directly. It forms when sunlight reacts with other gases, so it's highest on hot, sunny afternoons.

script.speaker: tara
script.text: Sulphur dioxide?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: That comes mainly from industry, particularly from burning coal, although levels have fallen a lot in this country.

script.speaker: tara
script.text: Fine particles?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: In winter, many of those come from wood burning in homes, which surprised me.

script.speaker: tara
script.text: And the coarse dust?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: From building sites, where cement and soil are disturbed.

script.speaker: tara
script.text: That's enough for the section. I'll send you my draft tonight.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the Dead Sea
parts.context: A geography lecture on the Dead Sea and its problems.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the Dead Sea. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. Today I'd like to talk about one of the most unusual stretches of water in the world: the Dead Sea. It is really a salt lake, and it lies between Jordan to the east and Israel to the west.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Its shore is about four hundred and thirty metres below sea level, which makes it the lowest dry land on Earth.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The water is about nine times as salty as the ocean. Because it is so dense, people float on it without any effort, and you can read a newspaper while lying on the surface. But very little can live in it. Only a few kinds of bacteria and one or two tiny organisms survive, and that is where the name comes from.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The lake is fed mainly by the River Jordan, and it has no outlet. Water leaves only by evaporation, which in the hot desert climate is very fast, so the salt is left behind and gradually builds up.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Today the Dead Sea is in trouble. Its level is falling by about a metre every year. The main reason is that most of the water of the Jordan and its tributaries is diverted for agriculture and for drinking, so far less flows in than before. Mineral companies also pump water from the lake to extract salts, which makes the situation worse.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: As the water retreats, it leaves behind salt layers underground, which dissolve when fresh water reaches them. The ground then collapses, creating sinkholes along the shore, some of them large enough to swallow a road.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: One proposal is to build a canal from the Red Sea, to bring in water and stabilise the level. It would be very expensive, and some scientists worry that mixing the two kinds of water could change the lake's colour and chemistry. The debate continues. Next week we'll look at the Aral Sea.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
